methodology: Dated editorial synthesis. Confidence labels concern direction, not measured probabilities. Model identities follow repository labels and are not independently authenticated. See docs/RESEARCH.md.

models.name: Astra
models.strength: The clearest source trail and useful distinctions between technical progress and real-world deployment.
models.caution: Its practical-AGI date and robotics take-off are judgements, not conclusions established by its citations. Some energy numbers now have a newer edition.

models.name: Fable
models.strength: Makes its big bets explicit: rapid automation, a capital-spending correction and political fights over the gains.
models.caution: Specific market falls, elections, growth rates and catastrophe odds are not calibrated or independently supported. The document calls itself Claude.

models.name: Grok
models.strength: Pays attention to conflict, finance, reliability and the gap between a prototype and an economic product.
models.caution: The asserted one-in-three Taiwan invasion risk by 2028 is unattributed. A named danger window should not be mistaken for an expert consensus.

models.name: Gemini
models.strength: Adds useful breadth: infrastructure, sovereign computing, materials, authentication and public services.
models.caution: Many exact dates and claims of dominant or universal adoption have no source trail. Treaty, health and lunar-habitation milestones are especially speculative.

ai.title: AI Index 2026 · Technical performance
ai.note: Documents agent progress and persistent failures. Benchmarks do not establish autonomous job replacement or an AGI date.

jobs.title: Generative AI and jobs: A 2025 update
jobs.note: One in four workers is in an occupation with some exposure. This measures task exposure, not a forecast that one in four jobs disappears.

energy.title: Key Questions on Energy and AI · Executive summary
energy.note: Estimates data-centre electricity use at 485 TWh in 2025 and projects 950 TWh in 2030. Updates the older 945 TWh projection used by Astra.

electricity.title: Electricity 2026 · Executive summary
electricity.note: Projects 3.6% annual demand growth for 2026–30 and roughly half of generation from renewables plus nuclear in 2030.

ev.title: Global EV Outlook 2026 · Executive summary
ev.note: Projects electric-car adoption and a wider EV fleet reaching as many as 510 million by 2035, excluding two- and three-wheelers. EV definitions include plug-in hybrids.

climate.title: Global Annual to Decadal Climate Update 2026–2035
climate.note: Gives a 91% chance of at least one year above 1.5°C in 2026–30 and an 86% chance of a new annual record. These are not long-term Paris-threshold probabilities.

population.title: World Population Prospects 2024 · Population trends
population.note: 63 countries and areas, containing 28% of the 2024 population, had already peaked in population. Many other places continue growing.

artemis.title: Artemis III mission in 2027: crew and mission details
artemis.note: NASA targets an Earth-orbit test for Artemis III in 2027 and an Artemis IV lunar landing in 2028. These are plans, not guaranteed delivery dates.

pqc.title: Post-Quantum Cryptography · Migration timeline
pqc.note: Quantum-vulnerable algorithms are due to leave NIST standards by 2035, with high-risk systems moving earlier. This is not a global completion deadline.

quantum.title: IBM Quantum Roadmap
quantum.note: Targets Starling in 2029 and a larger Blue Jay system in 2033+. A vendor roadmap establishes ambition, not successful commercial advantage.

nato.title: Defence investment and the 5% commitment
nato.note: The 2035 framework combines at least 3.5% of GDP for core defence with up to 1.5% for broader security and resilience. Delivery remains political.

odni.title: 2026 Annual Threat Assessment · Taiwan, p. 22
odni.note: Assesses no current Chinese plan for a 2027 invasion or fixed unification timetable, while recognising force capabilities and escalation risks. This is one government’s assessment.

imf.title: World Economic Outlook Update, July 2026
imf.note: Projects 3.0% global growth in 2026 and 3.4% in 2027, with conflict and market-repricing risks. It does not forecast a 2035 AI boom.

gene.title: Gene therapy approval for young children with sickle cell disease
gene.note: Casgevy’s expanded indication demonstrates real progress in specific genetic conditions. It does not establish general longevity or common-disease cures.

education.title: Guidance for generative AI in education and research
education.note: Emphasises human involvement, age-appropriate use, privacy and pedagogical validation. It does not predict a year of universal AI tutoring.

provenance.title: Content Credentials · Technical specification 2.2
provenance.note: Provides a mechanism to authenticate media provenance. Adoption, preserved metadata and trusted signers remain essential.

fusion.title: Office of Fusion · Science and Technology Roadmap
fusion.note: Aims to enable a US fusion pilot power plant in the mid-2030s. A pilot is distinct from cheap, repeatable, large-scale commercial generation.

adaptation.title: Adaptation Gap Report 2025
adaptation.note: Estimates developing-country adaptation needs at $310bn–$365bn annually in 2035, against $26bn in international public flows in 2023. The measures and years differ.

years.title: AI leaves the chat window.
years.summary: Expect more software that completes work. The hard part becomes trusting it with the next step.
years.watch: Look for completed workflows with fewer human interventions, rather than better demonstrations.
takes: Useful multi-hour agents; software teams reorganise.
Reliable multi-day agents already; early hiring pressure.
Back-office automation grows, constrained by the real economy.
Routine workflows shift predominantly to autonomous agents.

events.title: From assistant to colleague
events.summary: Agents handle larger parts of coding, support and administration. People still supervise exceptions, permissions and important decisions.
events.why: The productivity gain comes from finishing an entire workflow. A system that saves drafting time but needs constant repair may save little overall.
events.evidence: Stanford reports substantial computer-task progress alongside frequent failures; the ILO expects job transformation to be more common than full replacement.
events.watch: Independently measured completion rates, total supervision time and entry-level hiring.
events.caveat: We soften Fable’s reliable multi-day claim and Gemini’s predominantly autonomous claim. Capability does not guarantee adoption.

events.title: The bottleneck is the connection
events.summary: Access to electricity, chips and financing increasingly determines where new computing capacity can actually open.
events.why: Fast-growing demand meets infrastructure that takes years to permit and build. Regions with spare capacity gain an advantage.
events.evidence: The IEA’s 2026 update identifies tighter grid, equipment and chip constraints.
events.watch: Energised capacity, transformer delivery times and cancelled projects.
events.caveat: Local shortages can be severe even while data centres remain a small share of global electricity use.

events.title: A recovery with fault lines
events.summary: Modest global growth is more plausible than an immediate AI-led boom. War, energy costs and debt can overwhelm technological gains.
events.why: Technology investment supports some economies while expensive imports and weak public finances hold others back.
events.evidence: The IMF projects 3.4% global growth in 2027 in its July 2026 update.
events.watch: Inflation, energy trade disruption, investment returns and business spending.
events.caveat: This is a revisable institutional forecast, not certainty. We do not carry its growth rate into the 2030s.

years.title: The demo meets the real world.
years.summary: Useful automation spreads unevenly. Trust, physical reliability and geopolitical restraint matter as much as raw capability.
years.watch: Look for paid renewals and dependable operating hours, not shipment announcements alone.
takes: Persistent agents; industrial robots; no invasion in the base case.
AI correction of 30–40%; capabilities keep advancing.
Taiwan crisis risk peaks; robotics begins affecting selected sectors.
Viable humanoids, a binding orbital treaty and new battery milestones.

events.title: Robots earn their place on a shift
events.summary: Expect more useful robots in controlled workplaces before broadly capable machines in ordinary homes.
events.why: A repetitive environment can make a narrow robot valuable. Homes demand much more versatility and safety at a price households can afford.
events.evidence: Stanford’s 2026 review finds a large gap between controlled robotic tasks and real household success.
events.watch: Paid deployment renewals, intervention rates and cost per productive hour.
events.caveat: There is no well-supported year when general humanoids become a universal economic substitute for workers.

events.title: Seeing needs a source
events.summary: Synthetic media increases the value of verified origins, known publishers and secure identity checks. Provenance helps; it does not settle truth.
events.why: Scams and disputed recordings impose costs even when nobody can reliably identify a fake by sight.
events.evidence: C2PA already specifies signed provenance for digital content.
events.watch: Camera and platform support, retained credentials and real verification habits.
events.caveat: A genuine recording can mislead; absent credentials do not prove a fake. Mandatory universal adoption is not established.

events.title: Taiwan remains a risk, not a date
events.summary: Continued pressure is the central scenario. Blockade, conflict and miscalculation remain consequential alternatives at any point in the decade.
events.why: A crisis could disrupt semiconductor supply, shipping, investment and the political assumptions behind the whole timeline.
events.evidence: The 2026 US intelligence assessment does not identify a current plan for a 2027 invasion or a fixed timetable.
events.watch: Sustained mobilisation, shipping restrictions, civilian preparations and working crisis communications.
events.caveat: This is a judgement, not a quantified risk estimate. Grok’s unattributed one-in-three claim is not adopted.

years.title: Progress gets a reality check.
years.summary: Some investments disappoint even as the technology improves. Lunar ambitions and financial expectations face delivery tests.
years.watch: Separate money raised, hardware demonstrated and services actually delivered.
takes: AI investment shakeout around 2028–30; Moon landing in 2029.
Remote-worker AI; UK/US SMRs; Moon landing in 2029–30.
Robot economics improve; lunar return pushed to around 2030.
Late-stage AI drugs; sovereign computing and storage spread.

events.title: A shakeout is plausible
events.summary: An AI investment correction could arrive while usage continues growing. Its date, size and market winners are unknowable in advance.
events.why: Expensive assets need sustained revenue. A useful technology can still attract more capital than its early earnings justify.
events.evidence: The IEA flags capital-market dependence; the IMF identifies financial repricing as a risk.
events.watch: Utilisation, cash generation, refinancing costs and customers renewing paid contracts.
events.caveat: We retain the scenario but reject a scheduled crash or an unsupported 30–40% fall as the central forecast.

events.title: The Moon moves within reach
events.summary: A crewed lunar return in the late 2020s or early 2030s is plausible. It remains a difficult programme, with delay risk.
events.why: Docking, landers, life support and the launch sequence all have to work together. A successful mission could restart repeated exploration.
events.evidence: NASA targets an Artemis III Earth-orbit test in 2027 and an Artemis IV landing in 2028.
events.watch: Integrated demonstrations, lander readiness and sustained programme funding.
events.caveat: 2029 is our window’s centre, not NASA’s announced date. It is not a guaranteed milestone.

events.title: A ceasefire is not a settlement
events.summary: A prolonged armed stand-off in Ukraine and recurring Middle East disruption remain plausible even if intense fighting subsides.
events.why: Stopping major combat can be easier than settling territorial disputes or establishing security arrangements that every party accepts.
events.evidence: The IMF’s July 2026 outlook identifies war-related economic drag and renewed conflict as risks. It does not forecast peace dates.
events.watch: Verified and sustained ceasefires, security guarantees, civilian safety and reliable commercial shipping.
events.caveat: This is a synthesis of the originals, not an independently established geopolitical timetable. We retain neither a guaranteed armistice date nor a predicted regime collapse.

years.title: The future needs a bigger grid.
years.summary: Electrification is a stronger bet than any single breakthrough. More clean power and more climate damage can happen at the same time.
years.signal: The physical world sets the pace
years.watch: Track completed infrastructure, not just announcements or installed nameplate capacity.
takes: AI affects productivity; solar, EVs and data-centre demand expand.
Expert-level cognition; cold peace; long-term 1.5°C threshold crossed.
Power trade-offs; demographic stress; possible lunar return.
SMR commissioning and completed post-quantum migrations.

events.title: An increasingly electric economy
events.summary: Transport, cooling, industry and computation put more pressure on power systems. Cleaner generation expands, but fossil fuels remain important.
events.why: Electricity is the link between several changes that are often forecast separately. Transmission and flexibility matter alongside generation.
events.evidence: The IEA projects 3.6% annual electricity-demand growth and about half of generation from renewables plus nuclear in 2030.
events.watch: Grid additions, peak-demand management, battery use and delivered electricity costs.
events.caveat: The figures are scenario projections. A bigger low-carbon share is not the same as a fossil-free energy system.

events.title: Records keep falling
events.summary: Expect repeated dangerous heat and rising adaptation needs. We cannot responsibly name a record year or an exact long-term threshold crossing.
events.why: The costs arrive through health, water, agriculture, infrastructure and insurance, with very unequal exposure.
events.evidence: WMO gives an 86% chance of a new annual heat record during 2026–30 and a 91% chance of at least one year above 1.5°C.
events.watch: Multi-year temperature trends, heat exposure and financed adaptation.
events.caveat: An individual hot year is not a long-term Paris Agreement threshold breach. Fable’s exact 2030 placement is not retained.

events.title: Productivity gains, unevenly shared
events.summary: AI-led firms may produce more with smaller teams. Whole-economy gains probably arrive unevenly as organisations change how they work.
events.why: Cheaper individual tasks help only if firms can reorganise processes, maintain quality and find demand for the extra output.
events.evidence: The ILO distinguishes task exposure from redundancy; the IMF recognises technology investment alongside persistent economic risks.
events.watch: Output per hour, median wages, firm-level margins and new business creation.
events.caveat: Fable’s specific 2031 US growth rate and 2035 global boom are upside bets, not a defensible central path.

years.title: Capability is only half the story.
years.summary: The question becomes where powerful tools are reliable, affordable and allowed to operate.
years.watch: Ask what a system completes, how often it fails and who carries responsibility.
takes: Median practical-AGI date; specialised AI throughout medicine.
Measured productivity breakout; health screening; bio/cyber scare.
Labour-market division; first meaningful fusion pilot.
Autonomous trucking dominates designated corridors; routine orbital manufacturing.

events.title: AGI is still a disputed milestone
events.summary: Broadly capable digital systems are plausible in the early 2030s. A precise arrival year and a single decisive test are much weaker claims.
events.why: Competence across tasks does not automatically deliver reliable long-horizon work, independent learning or responsibility for real consequences.
events.evidence: Current evaluations show both impressive performance and uneven capabilities. They do not establish a trend that guarantees AGI.
events.watch: Novel-task transfer, long-horizon reliability and independent evaluations with real costs.
events.caveat: Astra’s 2031 median and Fable’s earlier trajectory are hypotheses. Plateau or slower progress remains possible.

events.title: More diseases become treatable
events.summary: Gene and cell therapies plausibly expand across specific conditions. Access, manufacturing and long-term safety may limit their everyday impact.
events.why: A treatment breakthrough matters only when patients can receive it safely and health systems can deliver and fund it.
events.evidence: The FDA’s 2026 Casgevy expansion is a concrete example of progress in defined genetic disorders.
events.watch: Clinical outcomes, eligibility, manufacturing capacity and treatment access.
events.caveat: This evidence does not support routine anti-ageing treatment, universal cancer cures or guaranteed common-disease gene editing by 2029.

events.title: Autonomy grows by geography
events.summary: Driverless transport expands in suitable operating areas. Weather, local rules, economics and difficult edge cases keep adoption patchy.
events.why: A dependable service in one city or freight corridor can be valuable without solving every road everywhere.
events.evidence: Stanford documents substantial autonomous-taxi deployment alongside geographically constrained operating conditions.
events.watch: Independent safety data, operating coverage, fares and remote-assistance needs.
events.caveat: Gemini’s dominant interstate-freight share by 2031 is a stronger claim than the evidence supports.

years.title: Automation reaches beyond the desk.
years.summary: More physical tasks become economic to automate. Schools and care systems still revolve around people.
years.watch: Look for durable improvements to daily services, not just more devices.
takes: Robotics take-off; imperfect home robots; SMRs begin to matter.
AI tutors standard; oil peak behind us; homes still niche.
More automated factory cells; Earth-orbit business grows.
Routine preventive genomics; resilient microgrids; diversified minerals.

events.title: A broader working life for robots
events.summary: Mobile robots and manipulators spread in logistics, hospitals and commercial facilities. General domestic help remains a harder market.
events.why: Repetition, labour shortages and workable layouts can justify machines that would still struggle in a cluttered home.
events.evidence: The gap between household and controlled-task performance remains visible in current robotics evaluations.
events.watch: Fleet uptime, worker outcomes, intervention frequency and service costs.
events.caveat: We do not assume a single robotics “moment” or treat all mobile machines as humanoids.

events.title: Tutoring gets more personal
events.summary: Adaptive voice and visual learning support becomes easier to access. Its value depends on teaching quality, safety and measured learning.
events.why: Affordable practice could help many learners, but schools also provide relationships, care and social development.
events.evidence: UNESCO calls for human-centred, age-appropriate design and educational validation.
events.watch: Learning outcomes against credible comparisons, accessibility and teacher workload.
events.caveat: Wide availability does not establish benefit. Universal use or disappearing qualifications is not assumed.

events.title: Firm clean power has a bigger role
events.summary: Some new nuclear and geothermal projects may begin serving industrial demand. Large fleets of cheap new reactors remain less certain.
events.why: Variable renewable supply increases the value of flexibility and dependable low-carbon output, but construction economics still decide deployment.
events.evidence: The IEA projects rising nuclear output through 2030, alongside renewables and natural gas.
events.watch: Projects completed on budget, licensing progress and contracted delivered power costs.
events.caveat: No claim is made that every announced small reactor is operational by 2030, or that a power contract proves one exists.

years.title: Discovery starts to accelerate.
years.summary: AI can shorten parts of research. The distance from a promising result to a useful product still matters.
years.watch: Track replicated discoveries, engineering scale-up and products that reach users.
takes: AI scientific collaborators; narrow quantum usefulness.
Automated research pays off; fusion electricity demonstration.
Very lean agent-based firms; political succession uncertainty.
Autonomous labs; AR displaces phones; supersonic travel expands.

events.title: Faster loops in the laboratory
events.summary: AI and automated experiments may speed discovery in materials and chemistry. The gains will differ sharply between fields.
events.why: Research systems become more valuable when predictions are checked by experiments and the results feed the next investigation.
events.evidence: The IEA identifies AI-led industrial innovation as a potential long-term source of productivity gains.
events.watch: Replicated results, experiment throughput and commercially useful new materials.
events.caveat: A faster discovery stage does not remove clinical trials, manufacturing limits or engineering qualification.

events.title: Quantum advantage stays specialised
events.summary: Fault-tolerant hardware could unlock useful scientific applications. A timetable for broad commercial value is still speculative.
events.why: Error-corrected computation must be large, reliable and competitive with improving classical alternatives.
events.evidence: IBM targets a 200-qubit Starling system in 2029 and a larger system in 2033+. These are vendor milestones.
events.watch: Independent end-to-end advantage, error-corrected workload size and total cost.
events.caveat: A roadmap is evidence of intent. It is not evidence that a practical quantum breakthrough has happened.

events.title: Adaptation becomes core infrastructure
events.summary: Cooling, flood protection and water resilience take a larger place in public budgets, with the largest gaps often where resources are weakest.
events.why: Repeated disruption can shift the question from whether to adapt to which protections can actually be financed.
events.evidence: UNEP finds a large shortfall between developing-country adaptation needs and international public finance.
events.watch: Completed protection, heat mortality, water security and insured versus uninsured losses.
events.caveat: We reject an exact year for a particular disaster or a $500bn single-event loss.

years.title: The hardest problems are human.
years.summary: Ageing, distribution and security determine who benefits from new capabilities. Better tools do not settle political choices.
years.watch: Watch who gains time, income and access—not only how much output rises.
takes: AI-assisted R&D; new ways to distribute gains; adaptation grows.
More capable public services; great-power crisis; healthspan gains.
Early advanced-energy plants; service robots; drone-heavy militaries.
Home robots, fusion tests, digital trade and geoengineering pilots.

events.title: Care becomes a central economic need
events.summary: Older populations increase pressure on care, pensions and staffing across much of Europe and East Asia. Automation helps with tasks, not every relationship.
events.why: These pressures are already partly determined by existing age structures. They interact with migration, participation and public spending.
events.evidence: UN projections show many populations already shrinking while others, including much of sub-Saharan Africa, continue to grow.
events.watch: Care vacancies, healthy life expectancy, participation rates and service access.
events.caveat: This is a regional pattern, not a claim that the world population contracts this decade.

events.title: Who gets the productivity dividend?
events.summary: Tax, competition, training and working-time reforms become more prominent if AI gains concentrate among a small set of owners and firms.
events.why: More output can translate into higher wages, lower prices, shorter hours or higher profits. Institutions shape the split.
events.evidence: Labour-exposure evidence supports pressure for adaptation; it does not determine the policy response.
events.watch: Median disposable incomes, labour’s income share, market concentration and access to retraining.
events.caveat: Universal basic income, a four-day week and compute taxes are possible responses, not scheduled global outcomes.

events.title: Security competes for the same resources
events.summary: Defence and resilience remain major investment priorities, even if active wars subside. Fiscal trade-offs persist.
events.why: People, industrial capacity and funding used for security are also needed for infrastructure, care and climate resilience.
events.evidence: NATO’s 2035 spending framework includes core defence and wider security investment.
events.watch: Delivered capability, resilience of supply chains and credible multi-year budgets.
events.caveat: A commitment is not proof of delivery. We do not assign a specific year to a new great-power crisis or a leader’s succession.

years.title: Promises become measurable.
years.summary: Roadmaps converge on the mid-2030s. The useful question is which have become working systems.
years.watch: Distinguish a prototype, a repeatable product and meaningful system-wide adoption.
takes: Post-quantum transition; large EV fleet; fusion pilot and lunar presence.
4–5% global growth; tens of millions of humanoids; possible Mars launch.
Uneven productivity phase change; demography and strategic rivalry.
Automated preventive care and construction; continuously inhabited Moon.

events.title: The cryptography transition matures
events.summary: Quantum-resistant systems become increasingly normal, although legacy technology and slow migrations leave uneven coverage.
events.why: Sensitive data may need protection well before a cryptographically relevant quantum computer exists. Replacing infrastructure takes time.
events.evidence: NIST plans to remove quantum-vulnerable algorithms from its standards by 2035, with high-risk systems moving sooner.
events.watch: Inventories of vulnerable systems, tested interoperability and completed migrations.
events.caveat: This is not the date quantum computers break the internet, or a universal legal deadline for every organisation.

events.title: Fusion may reach the pilot stage
events.summary: A credible pilot delivering electricity is possible by the mid-2030s. Cheap fusion at a scale that changes the global energy mix is a much larger leap.
events.why: The challenge extends beyond fusion reactions to durable materials, reliable plant operations, fuel supply and cost.
events.evidence: The US DOE roadmap aims to enable a pilot plant in the mid-2030s.
events.watch: Net electricity at the plant boundary, uptime, maintenance and credible construction economics.
events.caveat: We separate net fusion energy, net electricity and economically competitive generation. The original forecasts often compress these steps.

events.title: A much larger electric fleet
events.summary: EVs account for far more road travel, with substantial regional differences. Replacing the existing vehicle stock takes longer than changing new sales.
events.why: Charging, vehicle prices, electricity costs and industrial policy shape adoption. Road electrification does not end oil demand in every other use.
events.evidence: IEA scenarios put the wider global EV fleet as high as 510 million in 2035, excluding two- and three-wheelers.
events.watch: Affordable models, charging reliability and the share of kilometres driven electrically.
events.caveat: The upper scenario is not a guaranteed count. Fleet size, new-car sales and battery-only cars are different measures.

years.title: More capable. Still complicated.
years.summary: The central picture is a more automated, more electric and more climate-exposed world. Its prosperity and stability remain choices, not technological inevitabilities.
years.watch: Judge the decade by lived outcomes: health, security, time, opportunity and shared prosperity.
takes: AI is embedded infrastructure; robots common; scarcity persists.
Cognition becomes abundant; control of compute defines politics.
Richer, hotter, automated and multipolar; no Mars residents.
Neural interfaces, resilient cities and a fragmented internet.

events.title: AI becomes ordinary infrastructure
events.summary: Capable software is woven into work and daily services. Human trust, judgement, care and accountability remain valuable.
events.why: The largest effect may be cheaper and more accessible services rather than a single recognisable “AGI event”.
events.evidence: Current AI deployment and labour research support transformation, while leaving its scale uncertain.
events.watch: Quality-adjusted service prices, access, working hours and independent measures of reliability.
events.caveat: The broad direction is more defensible than a post-scarcity claim. Cognitive abundance does not make housing, care or energy free.

events.title: Several futures coexist
events.summary: Countries and households experience very different decades depending on institutions, education, reliable power and access to capital.
events.why: A single global average can hide thriving regions, stagnation and severe local losses. Technology diffusion is neither immediate nor equal.
events.evidence: UN population projections already describe divergent demographic paths; current macro forecasts remain uneven.
events.watch: Median living standards, public-service access and whether less-connected regions share the gains.
events.caveat: No defensible model can name election winners, guarantee peace or give precise 2036 GDP from this evidence.

events.title: Physical limits still count
events.summary: More electrification and technical capability coexist with climate damage, scarce land, infrastructure needs and geopolitical tension.
events.why: Progress can reduce costs without removing every constraint. The quality of public decisions affects how far the gains spread.
events.evidence: Energy and adaptation outlooks point to large investment needs even as technology improves.
events.watch: Resilient power and water, emissions, adaptation outcomes and conflict avoidance.
events.caveat: A major war, pandemic, financial crisis or AI surprise could move the entire path. None is given a fabricated date.

comparisons.label: A pause is not a durable peace
takes: Ukraine armistice around 2028, plus or minus a year; Iran hostilities ease in 2027.
Ukraine ceasefire line in 2027, with continuing low-intensity conflict; weakened Iran.
Ukraine de facto freeze by 2028; recurring Middle East confrontation and shipping disruption.
No direct forecast of a Ukraine settlement or the Iran conflict.
comparisons.verdict: Ceasefire and unresolved conflict are plausible scenarios. None of these texts can establish a war’s end date; regional escalation could change the entire economic forecast.

comparisons.label: Same direction, different speed
takes: Practical AGI median around 2031; humans retain accountability.
Multi-day agents in 2027; expert cognition around 2028–30.
Major automation, but uneven productivity through 2035.
Predominantly autonomous routine work in 2027; no explicit AGI date.
comparisons.verdict: Retain rapid task automation as a plausible direction. Treat AGI dates, whole-job replacement and national growth impacts as separate, uncertain claims.

comparisons.label: Three discuss Taiwan directly
takes: No invasion in the central decade-long path.
No-war path is modal; reports roughly 25% war risk by 2036.
2028 crisis window; unattributed one-in-three invasion risk by end-2028.
Does not directly forecast Taiwan conflict.
comparisons.verdict: Absence is not agreement. Retain coercion as the central scenario and major conflict as a serious alternative; do not average incompatible, uncalibrated probabilities.

comparisons.label: Two explicit correction calls
takes: A substantial correction around 2028–30.
A 30–40% drawdown in 2028, with continued adoption.
Emphasises physical constraints and economics; no comparable dated crash.
Emphasises energy and debt constraints; no comparable dated crash.
comparisons.verdict: Investment disappointment is plausible. A precise crash year and magnitude add false precision, so the timeline treats this as a scenario.

comparisons.label: Controlled settings first
takes: Industrial deployment in 2028; wider take-off around 2032.
Cost-effective industrial robots around 2031; tens of millions by 2035.
Factory economics improve in 2029; homes remain mostly human.
Viable industrial humanoids in 2028; wealthy homes around 2034.
comparisons.verdict: The workplace-before-home sequence is credible. Installed units, human interventions and total costs matter more than a memorable launch year.

comparisons.label: Targets need careful reading
takes: Electricity bottlenecks; early SMRs around 2030–32; fusion pilot by 2035.
US/UK SMRs in 2029; fusion net electricity in 2033.
Fusion pilot in 2031; expensive early plants in 2034.
Modular deployments in 2027; commissioning in 2030; fusion tests in 2034.
comparisons.verdict: Keep the electricity constraint. Treat new nuclear and fusion dates as project-dependent windows; a contract, prototype and operating plant are different milestones.

comparisons.label: Direction clearer than the year
takes: New annual heat record likely around 2026–30; adaptation expands.
20-year average crosses 1.5°C in 2030; $500bn disaster in 2033.
More costly disasters and insurance retreat; 2°C becomes planning assumption.
Water stress, resilient infrastructure and possible geoengineering pilots.
comparisons.verdict: Warming and adaptation pressure are strongly supported. Exact disaster years, threshold dates and unilateral geoengineering are not placed in the central path.

comparisons.label: Some breakthroughs are over-specified
takes: Specific gene therapies and AI assistance; no general cure for ageing.
Common-condition gene editing in 2029; routine multi-cancer tests in 2031.
AI-designed drugs and modest longevity effects around 2031.
Routine preventive genomics by 2032; widespread neural assistance by 2036.
comparisons.verdict: Retain progress in specific treatments. Do not infer routine clinical benefit or mass access from early technical potential.

comparisons.label: Ambition is not evidence of delivery
takes: Lunar return in 2029; limited lunar presence and narrow quantum uses later.
Moon around 2029–30; roughly 40% chance of crewed Mars launch in 2035.
Moon around 2030; no one living on Mars in 2036.
Continuous lunar habitation and extraction by 2035.
comparisons.verdict: A lunar return is plausible; sustained habitation and crewed Mars are weaker bets. Quantum roadmaps remain vendor targets until independently demonstrated.
